papers.title: FIREQ: FPGA Instrumentation for Readout and Qubit control
papers.abstract: We present FIREQ (FPGA Instrumentation for Readout and Qubit control), an open-source RFSoC-based framework for the control and readout of superconducting qubits. FIREQ combines a modular AXI-compliant firmware architecture with a PYNQ-based software stack designed to support extensible hardware integration, deterministic experiment timing, and low-overhead execution of repeated calibration and characterization workflows. The firmware implements direct RF synthesis and acquisition, trigger-based sequencing, programmable pulse generation, frequency-multiplexed readout, and memory-efficient acquisition and waveform buffering. The software adopts a client-server architecture with streamed data transfer and dependency-aware configuration updates to reduce host-device and reconfiguration overhead during parameter sweeps. On an AMD Zynq UltraScale+ RFSoC ZCU216, FIREQ generates RF pulses up to 9.3 GHz with a pulse-duration resolution of 107 ps and an event-timing resolution of 1.7 ns. FPGA resource utilization is compared with representative open-source RFSoC control frameworks, showing a low BRAM footprint while retaining full-rate I/Q generation and acquisition. The RF output is characterized in terms of phase noise, noise spectral density, and inter-channel timing skew. End-to-end operation is validated on a superconducting qubit through resonator spectroscopy, Rabi, Ramsey, and relaxation measurements, yielding T1 = 6.94 us and T2* = 13.50 us. FIREQ can therefore be used both as a qubit-control platform and as an experimental environment for evaluating alternative control and readout IP architectures.

summary.summary: FIREQ is an open-source RFSoC-based framework for superconducting qubit control and readout implemented on an AMD Zynq UltraScale+ ZCU216, combining modular AXI-compliant firmware with a PYNQ-based software stack to achieve direct RF synthesis up to 9.3 GHz, 107 ps pulse-duration resolution, and 1.7 ns event-timing resolution. End-to-end validation on a superconducting qubit yields $T_1 = 6.94$ µs and $T_2^* = 13.50$ µs, with normalized resource utilization competitive with existing RFSoC frameworks while maintaining low BRAM footprint through envelope interpolation and memory-efficient buffering.
summary.motivation: Scaling superconducting quantum processors requires efficient control electronics that minimize interconnects and hardware cost per channel. FIREQ addresses the need for resource-efficient, extensible room-temperature control platforms suitable for both current instrumentation and future cryogenic integration.
summary.method: FIREQ employs a hardware-software co-design with trigger-based deterministic timing, programmable envelope generation with on-the-fly linear interpolation, frequency-multiplexed readout, and a client-server architecture with dependency-aware configuration updates to reduce host-device overhead during parameter sweeps.
summary.result: On the ZCU216, FIREQ generates RF pulses with phase noise below $-116$ dBc/Hz at 1 MHz offset (at 0.5 gain), inter-channel timing skew of $1.8 	ext{ ps}$ mean and $0.84$ ps standard deviation, and software overhead reducing from 26% for short sequences to $	hicksim 1	ext{–}1.5	ext{%}$ for longer experiments over millions of shots.

papers.title: Robust CZ gate against flux line memory
papers.abstract: High-fidelity CZ gates are central to superconducting quantum processors, but implementations based on flux tuning are still sensitive to pulse distortion. Conventional predistortion, typically used for an isolated gate, can recover the desired flux at the chip but it fails if the flux line memory exists, causing the fidelity of repeated CZ gates to drop rapidly. To address this issue, we model the flux line distortion as the dynamics of a stateful classical actuator coupled to a quantum system. Using a first-order Dyson expansion, we derive the error generators induced by variations in the initial flux-line state. We then design a robust CZ gate by optimizing the flux pulse to suppress these generators and minimize the residual flux line state at the gate exit. A one-pole flux line model shows the expected first-order robustness plateau. For a more practical three-pole model, the optimized CZ pulse achieves $F_{\mathrm{avg}}=99.998\%$, suppresses all first-order error generators, and brings the residual flux line state close to zero. With no additional waiting time between gates, our robust pulse achieves $F_{\mathrm{avg}}=99.97\%$ for the complete ten-gate sequence and reduces the sequence infidelity by a factor of about $2.3\times10^{3}$ relative to the baseline under the same predistortion protocol. These results show that explicitly accounting for flux line memory maintains high-fidelity CZ operation across repeated gate sequences and addresses a key limitation of conventional predistortion.

Above 99.9% Fidelity Single-Qubit Gates, Two-Qubit Gates, and Readout in a Single Superconducting Quantum Device

summary.summary: This work models flux line memory in superconducting qubit control as a stateful classical actuator coupled to the quantum system, deriving first-order error generators for each actuator state component using Dyson expansion. Robust CZ pulses are designed by suppressing these generators and minimizing residual flux line state at gate exit, achieving $F_\mathrm{avg}=99.998\%$ for single gates and $99.97\%$ over ten consecutive gates with $2.3\times10^3$ reduction in sequence infidelity versus baseline.
summary.motivation: Flux-tuned CZ gates in superconducting processors suffer from distortions in the control line that persists between gates; conventional predistortion assumes zero initial flux line state but fails when nonzero memory remains from prior gates, causing rapid fidelity degradation in repeated sequences.
summary.method: The flux line dynamics are modeled in state space and coupled to the QCQ Hamiltonian. First-order perturbation theory connects initial actuator state variations to quantum error generators via the free response of the actuator. Two boundary conditions are imposed: memory robustness suppresses first-order errors from inherited actuator state via vanishing logical and leakage generator components, while state closing constrains the residual actuator state written at gate exit to near zero.
summary.result: In a one-pole model, the robust pulse shows a clear first-order plateau up to $x_c\approx3.5\times10^{-3}\Phi_0$ then quartic error growth versus quadratic for baseline. In a three-pole model fitted to measured line response, a 50 ns pulse simultaneously suppresses all three modal error generators and achieves $99.97\%$ fidelity over ten consecutive gates without extra reset time, compared to $20.3\%$ for baseline under identical reuse conditions.

papers.title: Understanding the superconducting proximity effect in semiconductors through quantum oscillations
papers.abstract: Superconductor-semiconductor hybrids host emergent states of matter and offer a platform for new qubits, but the superconducting metal shunts electrical transport, which rules out conventional semiconductor characterization and leaves the hybrid parameters to speculation. Here we determine density, mass, $g$-factor, mobility and subband occupation beneath the superconductor, from Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations of a buried InAs quantum well under Al, Sn, V, Nb, Ta and Re films, with a Dingle analysis that accounts for the shunt. Every metal adds an interface subband whose occupation falls into one of two classes, whereas the mass and $g$-factor of the buried well are unchanged to within 10\%. Within the uncertainty set by the transport mobility, no film shortens the quantum lifetime of the buried well, and Al and Sn lengthen it. Quantum lifetimes bound the hybridization of the interface subband to 2-4~meV. These measurements supply the normal-state parameters that tunnelling spectroscopy renormalizes but cannot measure.

similar_to.title: Quasiparticle dynamics in epitaxial Al-InAs planar Josephson junctions

summary.summary: Quantum oscillations of a buried InAs quantum well beneath Al, Sn, V, Nb, Ta and Re films directly measure the semiconductor's normal-state parameters—density, mass, $g$-factor, mobility and quantum lifetime—that are renormalized but not accessible to tunnelling spectroscopy. Every metal creates a distinct interface subband with occupation falling into two classes determined by orbital character rather than work function, while the buried well's mass and $g$-factor remain invariant at $0.040\text{–}0.044\,m_e$ and $|g_\mathrm{eff}| = 4.9 \pm 0.2$ across all films, and its quantum lifetime either improves or remains unchanged.
summary.motivation: Superconductor–semiconductor hybrids require knowledge of the semiconductor's band structure, disorder and coupling strength beneath the superconductor, but the metal shunts electrical transport and blocks conventional Hall-bar characterization, forcing reliance on uncapped sister samples or spectroscopy that measure different systems.
summary.method: Shubnikov–de Haas oscillations on unpatterned In$_{0.75}$Ga$_{0.25}$As/InAs/In$_{0.75}$Ga$_{0.25}$As heterostructure stacks resolve the buried well and interface subbands; a corrected Dingle analysis accounts for the shunt prefactor $P = (\mu_t^2 B^2 - 1)/(1 + \mu_t^2 B^2)^2$ that produces non-monotonic envelopes, and spin-zero spectroscopy in tilted fields determines $|g|m^*/m_e$ model-free.
summary.result: Interface densities span $(5.3\text{–}6.5) \times 10^{11}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ for refractory metals and $(1.2\text{–}1.3) \times 10^{12}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$ for Al/Sn; quantum lifetimes yield upper bounds on escape rate $\Gamma_\mathrm{QW} \leq 0.18\text{–}0.6$ meV and induced-gap ceilings $\Delta_\mathrm{ind}^\mathrm{max} = 0.3\text{–}0.8\,\Delta_0$ for the buried well, constraining the quasiparticle weight $Z \geq 0.1\text{–}0.2$.
